note_claims.claim: The patient has a flare of atopic eczema lasting 2 weeks.
The patient's eczema flare duration was initially reported as a month but corrected to two weeks.
The patient experiences nocturnal itch that disturbs sleep.
The patient's eczema flare is worst in the flexures, specifically the right elbow.
The patient denies weeping, crusting, blisters, or punched-out lesions.
The patient has recently started using bubble baths.
The patient uses Epaderm once daily and hydrocortisone 1% cream.
The patient has no personal history of asthma or wheezing.
The patient's father has hay fever and her sister has asthma.
The patient uses Epaderm emollient and hydrocortisone 1% cream (over the counter).
The patient has dry, erythematous, excoriated patches in both antecubital and both popliteal fossae.
The right elbow crease is the most severe area of the rash.
There are no signs of infection (no weeping, crusting, or vesicles).
The condition is a moderate flare of atopic eczema with no signs of infection.
A possible trigger for the flare is bubble baths.
The plan is to use clobetasone butyrate 0.05% once daily for 7 days, followed by hydrocortisone 1% if needed.
The patient should use Epaderm 3–4 times daily and as a soap substitute (at least 500 g tub every 2 weeks).
The patient should stop using bubble baths.
The follow-up appointment is scheduled in two weeks.
The patient should seek same-day review if they develop painful sores, blisters, or punched-out spots, especially with fever or feeling unwell (possible eczema herpeticum).

transcript_facts.fact: The patient's eczema is flared up badly, causing nocturnal itch and sleep disturbance.
The patient's eczema flare duration was corrected from a month to two weeks.
The worst areas of the flare are the backs of the knees and the insides of the elbows, with the right elbow being the worst.
The patient reports the condition is very itchy.
The patient denies weeping, crusting, or yellow discharge, reporting only red, dry, and scratched skin.
The patient denies having blisters or painful sores that look like little punched-out holes.
The patient denies having fevers or feeling unwell.
The patient is currently using Epaderm once a day and hydrocortisone cream from the chemist.
The hydrocortisone cream strength is one percent.
The patient denies having any other medications or drug allergies.
The patient's father has hay fever and her big sister has asthma.
The patient has no personal history of asthma or wheezing.
The patient has a cat at home.
The patient has started having bubble baths at her mum's.
Examination findings show dry, red, scratched patches in both elbow creases and behind both knees, with the right elbow crease being the worst.
Examination findings show no weeping, crusting, or blisters, indicating no sign of infection.
The plan is to use clobetasone butyrate 0.05% once daily on the red patches for seven days, then switch back to hydrocortisone 1% if needed.
The clinician explained that the cream should be applied using a fingertip unit, covering an area the size of two adult hands.
The plan is to use Epaderm three or four times a day, at least a 500 gram tub every two weeks, and to use it as a soap substitute.
The patient is instructed to stop using bubble baths.
The clinician plans to review the patient in two weeks.
Safety netting advises seeking same-day review if the patient develops painful sores, blisters, or punched-out spots, especially with fever or feeling unwell (possible eczema herpeticum).
